extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians and philosophers of mathematics (researchers and graduate students interested in foundations, proof methodology, and philosophy of mathematical practice)
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and evaluate whether a mathematical proof meets historical and contemporary notions of ‘purity’ (e.g., topical/Aristotelian purity, avoidance of circularity, and matching method-generalities). Apply criteria about topic-conservation, method–theorem fit, and epistemic aims of proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aristotelian metabasis prohibition (no crossing of genera)
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Metabasis ex allo genos’ — the prohibition against passing from one genus to another in the course of a proof (e.g., ‘We cannot, for instance, prove geometrical truths by arithmetic’).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Motivation: conserves the subject-matter of a demonstrative proof and ensures the necessary middle term; violations do not make an argument worthless but mean it doesn’t provide highest/best knowledge. Note: Aristotle allows metabasis between a science and its subordinates (e.g., geometry used in mechanics). Anti-pattern: using methods belonging to an ‘alien’ genus to prove theorems of the target genus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conservation of topic (proofs should preserve the ‘what’ of the topic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs should proceed from prior knowledge of the ‘what’ of their subject; development by inference must conserve the topic so that the demonstration shows why the predicate holds of the subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is tied to Aristotle’s idea that demonstrative knowledge requires comprehension of the subject’s essence and that the proof should not introduce conceptual resources outside the thesis. Practical test: check whether intermediate concepts or methods introduced lie within the conceptual scope of the theorem statement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causal/essential grounding requirement (proofs must show why)
rubrics_metrics.description: A pure proof should reveal the necessary connection (the ‘cause’ or aitia) between the subject and predicate — i.e., show that the predicate follows from the subject’s essence or definition (‘the “why” is referred ultimately ... to the “what”’).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purity’s epistemic aim is to provide knowledge of the cause, not merely confirmation. In practice this favors proofs that reduce the conclusion to definitions/essences of the objects involved (e.g., definitions of straight line, commensurable). Anti-pattern: proofs that establish truth without revealing the essential reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery vs demonstration separation (discovery methods not substitutes for proof)
rubrics_metrics.description: Methods useful for discovery (e.g., mechanical or heuristic arguments) may be useful to find a theorem but are not themselves adequate as demonstrations (Archimedes: mechanical method made things clear but ‘had to be demonstrated by geometry afterwards’).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use discovery methods to generate conjectures or guide proofs, but provide a separate, acceptable form of demonstration in the target discipline. Anti-pattern: treating a mechanical/heuristic argument as a final proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generality-fit criterion (methods’ generality must match theorem’s generality)
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Purely analytic’ (Bolzano): use rules/methods independent of particular natures; the generality of methods used should fit the generality of the theorem proved (avoid importing geometry into a theorem about quantities generally).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test: if a theorem is stated as a general/arithmetic/analytic result, proofs appealing to special-domain facts (e.g., spatial/ geometric facts) are impure. Example: Bolzano’s objection to geometric proofs of the intermediate value theorem; he demands methods whose generality matches that of the theorem. Anti-pattern: appeals to ‘truths borrowed from geometry’ when the theorem is about general quantities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of circular grounding / preservation of objective ordering
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs should not invert the objective ordering of truths or ground a general theorem on a particular theorem that in fact depends on the general one (Bolzano’s concern that geometric proofs in analysis can introduce circularity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check whether the proposed dependencies actually reverse the correct ontological/epistemic priority; impure proofs may produce circular justification. Example: proving a general analytic theorem by a geometrical theorem that itself presupposes analytic facts. Anti-pattern: proofs that implicitly assume the result or its consequences in the auxiliary domain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between confirmatory and justificatory reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish proofs that merely confirm (Gewissmachung) from those that provide objective justification (objektive Begründung); purity aims at the latter — revealing objective reasons rather than only giving evident verification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the proof extends knowledge (reveals new underlying truths) or merely makes a proposition evident. Historical note: Bolzano and others emphasize that obviousness doesn’t relieve one of seeking proper proof. Pedagogic implication: prefer proofs that justify rather than merely demonstrate by example or picture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topical purity / ‘elementary’ proof criterion (proof rooted in concepts of the subject)
rubrics_metrics.description: A topical or ‘elementary’ proof proceeds from analysis of the central concept(s) of the theorem (e.g., Selberg/Erdős’ elementary proofs of the prime number theorem showing ‘analytic inevitability’ from the concept of prime, avoiding extraneous complex-analytic methods).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operational test: can the result be derived by argument staying within the conceptual resources native to the statement (e.g., arithmetic/combinatorics for arithmetic problems)? Purity here is judged by absence of appeals to techniques ‘remote from the problem itself.’ Benefit: provides conceptual insight tied to the subject-concept. Anti-pattern: proof that succeeds only by invoking heavy machinery remote from the statement’s core concepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specialist-conceptual purity (domain-authentic proofs for specialist communities)
rubrics_metrics.description: Within specialist fields (e.g., combinatorics), a proof is considered properly proved only if it uses the field’s native methods (Stanton & Zeilberger: ‘a combinatorial result is not properly proved until it receives a direct combinatorial proof’).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: such proofs give greater insight to specialists and are more useful for further work in the specialty. Practical implication: when evaluating a proof’s value to a community, prefer proofs that employ community-standard conceptual tools. Anti-pattern: translating a problem into another domain and proving it there when direct domain techniques exist or are desirable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purity’s pragmatic and pedagogic virtues (clarity, efficiency, and extendability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Purity tends to (i) reveal previously unnoticed truths (extending knowledge), (ii) improve efficiency by clarifying and ordering concepts, and (iii) facilitate pedagogy and subsequent development of theories (Bolzano and others argue purity increases reach and makes learning easier).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing a proof, consider its pedagogic clarity and whether it makes concepts clearer and more connected; purity can be valued for these instrumental epistemic gains even if not deemed strictly superior as justification. Example: Dedekind and others sought arithmetization to gain objectivity and pedagogic clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feasibility and topic-identification criterion (is a pure proof possible/appropriate?)
rubrics_metrics.description: Before demanding topical purity, one must judge what the problem is ‘about’ (e.g., real roots problem that ineliminably requires complex numbers — casus irreducibilis) and whether pure methods are available or ineliminable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a meta-criterion: evaluate whether the introduction of certain concepts is unavoidable for solving the problem. If certain techniques are ineliminable, insisting on purity may be misplaced. Practical test: analyze whether existing proofs necessarily invoke foreign concepts or whether reformulations allow purity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counter-ideal/competing-virtue awareness (purity vs efficiency/intuitive methods)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that purity is one ideal among others (Hilbert: purity is ‘subjective’; Klein: geometric intuition and efficiency are valuable); sometimes extraneous methods promote efficiency, discovery, or practical proof construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation should weigh purity against competing aims (efficiency, insight, accessibility). Historical examples: Hilbert’s and Klein’s defenses of using non-pure methods for broader understanding or practical efficiency. Anti-pattern: treating purity as the sole criterion and ignoring practical mathematical benefits of non-pure approaches.
